newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-No quick end in sight to current oil rally.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-No quick end in sight to current oil rally.

text.p: No quick end can be seen to a blistering oil market rally which has taken prices to post-Gulf War highs in a volatile market that could leap again as winter demand increases, oil analysts say.
Oil prices could rise by as much as $5 a barrel if last winter's frigid temperatures are repeated, some traders say.
London November futures for international benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude on Wednesday hovered around the $25 level it broke earlier this week for the first time since the 1990/1991 Gulf War.

Brent stands $9 above last year's level of this time and has added $7 in value since mid-June, driven by concern over tensions in the oil-rich Middle East and persistently low stocks of heating oil in key consumer markets in the United States and Europe.

"By the first quarter 1997 we could easily see Brent at $30 if the current trend continues. It is only the middle of autumn. There could be a panic when the winter hits," said Bo Van Wijk, vice president of energy derivatives at UBS in Zurich.
Van Wijk reckons that the price of gas oil (European heating oil) could hit $300 a tonne in the middle of winter from the current $233 price for November futures.

Fuelling Wednesday's 25-30 cent gains in crude oil was news overnight that stocks of distillates, mostly heating fuel and diesel, in the U.S. Northeast, the world's biggest heating oil consumer, stand at an alarming 43 percent below 1995 levels.

Heading into winter, the oil industry is expected to build stocks of heating fuel not deplete them. The declines, which come at a time when U.S. refineries are producing almost at capacity, leads analysts to conclude that demand is much higher than expected.

"It is quite a puzzle. Production is running very high and there has been no real stock buiding so it is blindingly obvious that demand is higher than we expected," said Mike Barry of Energy Market Consultants (EMC).

Global oil demand is forecast by the International Energy Agency to soar 1.7 million barrels per day (bpd) this year to 71.8 million bpd but some analysts believe the IEA estimate is about 200,000-300,000 bpd too low.
Heating oil stocks are running about 10 percent down on last year's already slim levels in both northwest Europe and the United States. Analysts say oil companies are partly to blame.
Keen to cut costs by holding low inventories, some refiners have been caught short in a scramble to replenish winter stocks.

"The market is faced with a big dilemma now. There is huge U.S. demand for distillates at a time that the stocks are too low on both sides of the Atlantic. There is a fantastic vulnerability to cold weather," said Geoff Pyne, energy economist at UBS in London.
The oil rally will likely cost consumers dearly to heat their homes this winter, traders said. It may have a knock-on effect on air fares since airlines use middle distillates to fuel their jets.

"Oil companies have chosen to minimise oil stocks which saves the oil industry money. But it also passes on risk to the consumer," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of oil trading at Bankers Trust International in London. But the higher than expected oil price -- analysts have been busy revising up sharply their oil price forecasts -- has brought in a substantial windfall for oil producers.
For the 11 members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the higher oil price should bring in a further $20-25 billion in export revenue.
"This has been a very good year for us indeed and we hope it gets better," said an OPEC official in Vienna.
